sections.h2: Which Caro office files Tuscola County deeds and mortgages?
sections.html:
The Register of Deeds works from Suite 400 of the Purdy Building at 125 W. Lincoln Street in Caro, MI 48723. Doors are open on weekdays between 8:00 a.m. and 4:30 p.m., except for a lunch closure from noon until 1:00 p.m. and on holidays. Call 989-672-3840 or write to registerofdeeds@tuscolacounty.org.

You can walk a document in or send it by post. A mailed packet needs the exact fee and a stamped return envelope. Cash, money orders and checks are all taken, but a check must show the account holder's name and the bank's name and address, and it cannot be stale. An incorrect amount gets the whole request rejected, so count twice before sealing the envelope.

Caro is the county seat and Vassar is the second city. Tuscola County lies in Michigan's Thumb, with the Cass River running through it and highways M-15, M-24, M-25, M-46, M-81 and M-138 carrying traffic.

sections.h2: What are the recording charges at the Tuscola County Register of Deeds?
sections.html:
One flat charge of $30.00 covers entering and recording a deed, mortgage, lis pendens, certified copy or any other instrument. Documents that discharge or assign several older records cost extra.

Tuscola County Register of Deeds fee schedule, taken from the office's Fees for Copies and Recording page
ServiceCharge
Recording a deed, mortgage, lis pendens or other instrument$30.00 flat
Each added liber and page to be assigned, discharged, indexed or posted$3.00 extra
Photocopy of a real estate record$1.00 a page
Certifying a copy$5.00 a document
State or federal tax lien search certificate$3.00 a name

Inside each recording fee, $4.00 is sent to the Michigan State Survey and Remonumentation fund. Fixture filings, state and federal liens, state deeds, plats and tax reversion documents are spared that $4.00. Pay for copies when you order them, and give the liber and page when requesting by mail.

sections.h2: Why does the County Treasurer see a warranty deed before the Register of Deeds does?
sections.html:
Michigan law (MCLA 211.135, cited on the office's fee page) wants proof that taxes are paid before certain documents are recorded. Warranty deeds, assignments of a land contract that carry a warranty clause, and condominium master deeds go to the Tuscola County Treasurer first. The Treasurer charges $5.00 to certify.

After the stamp comes back, forward the papers to the Register of Deeds in the sequence they should be recorded, with the exact recording fee. Questions about certification go to the Treasurer at 989-672-3890.

Sellers with unpaid tax feel this step most. Ask the title company or closing attorney who is ordering the certificate, and do it early, since a mailed round trip adds days.

sections.h2: Which formatting rules can get a Tuscola County document returned?
sections.html:
The office checks every submission against the statutes it lists on its Recording Requirements page, beginning with MCL 565.201. A document that fails any one is returned.

  • Signatures in original ink, with the signer's name typed or printed below. Faxes and photocopies are refused.
  • An acknowledgement from a notary, judge or court clerk when the paper conveys or encumbers Michigan land.
  • A street or post office address for each grantee, and the drafter's name and address.
  • Black type of at least 10 points on white paper, between letter and legal size, with 2 1/2 inches blank at the top of page one and 1/2 inch elsewhere.
  • Only the last four digits of any Social Security number.
  • A single recordable event per instrument, named on the first printed line.

Certified copies are the only form of court order or death certificate accepted. Staff do not draft deeds, answer legal questions or hand out blank forms.

sections.h2: Which transfer taxes come due when a Tuscola County deed is recorded?
sections.html:
A recorded sale triggers both a county and a state charge. Under MCL 207.504, counties below 2,000,000 residents levy 55 cents for every $500 of value, and a part of $500 counts as a full unit. MCL 207.525 sets the state levy at $3.75 for each $500 or fraction.

The deed has to show the property's total value, or an affidavit of value must go with it. The Recording Requirements page adds that the tax is figured on the whole consideration unless the document names a valid exemption.

  • Under both acts, a price below $100, a security instrument, a lease, and some land contracts are exempt.
  • MCL 207.526 also lets a parent give property to a child, stepchild, grandchild or step-grandchild free of the state tax, and exempts foreclosure transfers.
  • The county list in MCL 207.505 omits the family exemption, so ask the office how the county share applies when a parent deeds a house to a child.

sections.h2: How do I find or protect records at the Tuscola County Register of Deeds?
sections.html:
Land record indexes are online from December 1988 to the present, and older records back to 1852 can be researched in the office. Indexes run by grantor and grantee name. The office cannot search by property address or parcel number, and it cannot say when a house was built, since its records cover land only.

Anyone may buy a copy of a recorded document, because recorded documents are public. A free Property Alert service emails you when a document in your name is recorded. The office says it is an alert and not fraud prevention, and a common name can trigger false alarms. Write to or call the office if an alert shows a document you do not recognize.

The register will not do title searches beyond simple ones, and the staff cannot decide who owns a property. That legal conclusion belongs with an attorney or title company.

sections.h2: What if the property taxes on a Tuscola County house are behind?
sections.html:
The Tuscola County Treasurer helps owners with delinquent tax avoid foreclosure and lists options to keep the property, sell it or let foreclosure go ahead. A property in forfeiture is not yet foreclosed. The office adds a title search fee of at least $175 plus the recording fee, and interest rises to 18% (1.5% per month), retroactive to when the tax first became delinquent.

After a year in forfeiture, the property is foreclosed, the owner's interest and all liens are removed and the right to redeem ends. Foreclosed parcels are offered at auction, and the county says details usually appear in early August for the August and October sales. For a bill you dispute, call your township assessor, who also handles Principal Residence, veteran and poverty exemption questions.

Tuscola County had about 52,680 residents in 2025, 86.4% of occupied homes were owner-occupied, and the median value was $149,500 for 2020 to 2024. Median household income was $63,811 and the average commute is 29.6 minutes, a sign of how rural much of the county is.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Tuscola County?
faqs.a: The flat recording fee is $30.00 for a deed, mortgage, lis pendens or other instrument, plus $3.00 for each additional liber and page. Transfer tax is separate and is collected on the total consideration unless an exemption is stated.

faqs.q: Do I need a tax certificate before recording a warranty deed in Tuscola County?
faqs.a: Yes. Send the document to the Tuscola County Treasurer first with the $5.00 certification fee, then submit the stamped document to the Register of Deeds with exact recording fees. The Treasurer's phone is 989-672-3890.

faqs.q: Can I look up a Tuscola County deed by address?
faqs.a: No. The office is not set up to index by address or parcel number. Search by grantor or grantee name, or give the liber and page, and online indexes start December 1, 1988.

faqs.q: Who can get a copy of a recorded Tuscola County deed?
faqs.a: Anyone can, because a recorded document is public. Copies cost $1.00 per page, a certification adds $5.00 per document, and mail requests need a self-addressed stamped envelope.

faqs.q: What are Michigan's transfer tax rates in Tuscola County?
faqs.a: The county rate is 55 cents per $500 of value and the state rate is $3.75 per $500. Both apply to the total value stated on the instrument or in an attached affidavit.
